extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, storytellers, and filmmakers (writers of dramatic fiction/screenplays)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing cinematic story structure: creating a credible character/plot interlock, composing the culminating climax, finding the Premise and Controlling Idea, and shaping progressions of Idea vs Counter-Idea to produce aesthetic emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven versus mere characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Character-driven’ often is mistaken for surface-level 'characterization driven'—tissue-thin portraiture (well-drawn mask) that lacks deep, expressed character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True character-driven work interlocks deep character with structure; avoid shallow portraiture whose mask is well drawn but inner life underdeveloped and unexpressed. Evaluate whether character choices actively propel the plot and reveal interior truth rather than merely decorating scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax and last act must be the most satisfying
rubrics_metrics.description: A film’s last act and Story Climax must deliver the most gratifying, meaningful experience; audiences judge a film by its final movement ('Movies are about their last twenty minutes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the final movement fails, the whole film collapses regardless of earlier success (examples: BLIND DATE vs KISS OF THE SPIDER WOMAN). Design the story so the climax is the pinnacle of emotional and intellectual payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate major design effort to the climax
rubrics_metrics.description: A finished screenplay represents 100% of the author's labor; most creative struggle goes into designing the interlock of deep character and event, and of that, the majority concentrates on creating the last-act climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to spend roughly three-quarters of story-design effort on character/event interlock and most of that on the climax. Treat the climax as the writer’s ultimate task—until it is created you don’t have the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax must be credible to the character’s established nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A thrilling climactic action may be invalidated if it contradicts the protagonist’s established characteristics (example: a 75-year-old hobbling accountant pursuing a three-day desert chase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the protagonist’s attributes (age, physicality, temperament, beliefs) make the climax believable; if not, rework characterization or the climax so deep character remains true while actions are credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacrifice any characterization that undermines credible action
rubrics_metrics.description: Any aspect of characterization that undermines the credibility of a climactic action must be sacrificed to preserve dramatic truth (GREED example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the integrity of the climax and story action even if it requires cutting or altering character details that would make the decisive action unbelievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is temporal art — save the best for last
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is a temporal medium (like music or dance) whose first commandment is to 'save the best for last'—the final movement/coda/climax should be the most meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think in terms of musical/symphonic architecture: pace the narrative so momentum builds to a culminating, most gratifying experience at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic emotion — unite idea and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Art (story) unites idea and emotion to produce 'aesthetic emotion'—a simultaneous encounter of thought and feeling that life seldom provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes so ideas are embodied in emotionally charged action; aim to produce moments that feel like epiphanies where idea and emotion fuse, rather than dry intellectual assertion or raw unmediated feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure as rhetoric — dramatize, do not explain
rubrics_metrics.description: A story should express and prove its ideas through events; master storytellers dramatize rather than explain or lecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid expository dialogue or authorial narration stating the thesis. Let the dynamics of events and human choice authenticate the idea. Example anti-pattern: characters explicitly stating 'crime doesn't pay' instead of the story showing it through consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise as open-ended source of inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: A Premise is the idea that inspires storytelling, often an open 'What would happen if...?' question rather than a closed statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premises can arise from dreams, facts, character bits, craft exercises or a glance out a window. Use them as springboards but do not treat them as sacred—abandon or alter the original premise if the evolving story requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise may spark but need not remain fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever inspires the writing need not stay in the writing; the Premise is not precious and may be left behind if the story evolves elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to follow the story’s evolution; the danger is stopping exploration because of attachment to initial inspiration. Writing is discovery—allow surprises and new directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling Idea — single-sentence Value plus Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The Controlling Idea (true theme) is a single coherent sentence expressing how and why life changes from the story’s beginning to its end; it consists of Value (positive/negative charge at climax) plus Cause (the primary reason for that change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate Controlling Idea from the climax by asking: 'What value results from this action?' and 'What chief cause produced that value?' Use this sentence to shape creative choices and to decide what is appropriate or irrelevant in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Controlling Idea to guide what to keep or cut
rubrics_metrics.description: The Controlling Idea shapes strategic choices; it tells you what is expressive of the story’s meaning (keep) versus what is irrelevant (cut).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tape the Value+Cause statement in view (Paddy Chayefsky technique) to resist extraneous detours. The clearer the controlling idea, the more unified and focused the story will be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive idea from action — do not impose idea on plot
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not draw action from idea; you draw idea from action. The story should tell you its meaning; the Controlling Idea should be discovered in the climax, not dictated beforehand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the climax and the character’s decisive action to reveal the controlling idea. If plot proceeds exactly as first planned without discovery, you may be over-controlling and stifling imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea versus Counter-Idea dynamic (Progressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective stories progress by dynamically moving between the positive Idea and its negative Counter-Idea, sequence by sequence, building a dialectical debate until one wins at climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose sequences that alternately affirm and contradict the central idea, increasing intensity until Crisis and then Climax. Example pattern in Crime films: scenes that imply 'crime pays' alternated with scenes that imply 'crime doesn't pay' until one prevails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build both sides with truth and intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: When staging the argument between Idea and Counter-Idea, craft the sequences supporting each side with equal seriousness and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pre-slant the narrative toward your preferred outcome. If the antagonist is weak, the protagonist’s victory rings false; if you intend a down-ending, make the opposing (positive) sequences convincing so the collapse feels earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didacticism — don't preach your idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs that aim merely to prove a writer’s idea risk becoming didactic/social-drama: thinly veiled sermons that stifle opposing voices and over-assert the remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and explore the Counter-Idea honestly; show the complexity and persistence of opposing forces (example: antiwar films that fail because they ignore the truth that 'men love war'). Let drama reveal truth rather than theatrical preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Controlling Ideas: idealistic, pessimistic, ironic
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories fall into three broad categories by emotional charge: Idealistic (up-ending: positive vision), Pessimistic (down-ending: negative vision), and Ironic (up/down simultaneously, both charges present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which charge you intend; use it to shape tone, sequence construction, and the dialectic between Idea and Counter-Idea. Examples: Idealistic — HANNAH AND HER SISTERS; Pessimistic — CHINATOWN; Ironic — ANNIE HALL, KRAMER VS. KRAMER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling Idea must express how and why change occurs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Controlling Idea is the purest statement of the story’s meaning: it states the value at climax and the chief cause producing that value, describing transformation from beginning to end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work backward from your climax to identify the dominant causal force (within character, society, or environment). Use that cause to keep scenes aligned with the story’s central logic and to avoid extraneous themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance protagonist and antagonist power to validate outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: To make either an up-ending or down-ending persuasive, the opposing force must be formidable enough that the protagonist’s victory (or defeat) feels earned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the antagonist is written as weak or foolish, the protagonist’s triumph will lack validity; conversely, if the antagonist is overwhelmingly powerful, a naive victory feels dishonest. Raise the stakes on both sides.
